newsitem.title: USA: Merger the inevitable solution to McDonnell's woes.
newsitem.headline: Merger the inevitable solution to McDonnell's woes.

text.p: After aerospace giant McDonnell Douglas Corp.'s commercial division slid from almost 50,000 to 14,000 employees in the 1990s, and then in November the company lost a huge military contract, the stage was set for dramatic change.
The direction of that change became clear with Sunday's announcement of a merger with the Boeing Co. to create the world's largest aerospace company.
At its peak, in 1990, McDonnell-Douglas Corp employed 136,000 people, including almost 50,000 at its commercial division.

But the end of the Cold War, weakness in the commercial sector and increased competition hurt business from all sides. Since 1990, the St. Louis-based company has halved its head count and its West Coast commercial division is a shadow of its former glory, with just 14,400 employees.

The decision in October to abandon development of the MD-XX widebody commercial jet, and the November loss of a U.S. military contract worth potentially $200 billion set the stage for Sunday's announcement, analysts said.

"McDonnell Douglas just didn't have the resources to aggressively fund its development programs," said Nick Heymann, an analyst at Natwest Securities. "They got stretched too thin on transports and fighters and commercial and they underinvested."
McDonnell Douglas employees said they were shocked by the merger announcement but that it makes sense.

"It's good for the company," said Dino Polimeropoulos, a cost and price analyst on McDonnell's F15 fighter program. He added that he expects layoffs among management and non-unionized, non-revenue-generating employees.
"It's probably a good thing. That way we'll be able to compete with Lockheed Martin," echoed a McDonnell engineer, referring to one of the company's chief competitors.
In Washington, Boeing officials said attempts will be made to reassign personnel to minimize layoffs. Currently McDonnell Douglas employs 65,000 people, including 24,000 in St. Louis.

Polimeropoulos, who works directly with McDonnell Douglas' suppliers, said they will likely be hurt by the deal. The company has been cutting back on the number of suppliers it uses to cut costs and has pressured employees to find the cheapest price and best quality for outsourced work, he said.
He speculated that the merger will intensify those trends as suppliers and sub-contractors are forced to compete with firms already serving Boeing.

McDonnell Douglas is the largest private employer in Missouri. Community officials expressed concern about the impact the deal will have, particularly in St. Louis where many small businesses have been hurt by the company's massive layoffs.

"This is always unsettling news," said Dennis Coleman, executive director of the St. Louis County Economic Council. "McDonnell Douglas had 42,000 employees here in 1989. They are down to about 22,000 employees now."

However, Murray Weidenbaum, chairman of the Center for the Study of American Business at Washington University and former chief economist for Boeing, said the deal could also have benefits for St. Louis.
Boeing has a better chance of landing the $200 billion U.S. fighter-jet contract, which is still up for grabs, with McDonnell Douglas on board, he speculated. That could mean more work for St. Louis.
"It's an opportunity and a threat to the St. Louis economy," he said.

He added that he does not expect the merger to fail on antitrust considerations, since Boeing specializes in airforce bombers and McDonnell Douglas in fighter aircraft. Commerical antitrust considerations are more significant but unlikely to derail the deal, he said.
Analysts said McDonnell Douglas had few options without the merger and would have been likely to become a niche player producing cargo aircraft for the commercial and military markets.
"This was done on Boeing's terms, for Boeing's benefit and will ultimately solve a lot of the problems of McDonnell Douglas," Heymann said.
McDonnell Douglas was created in 1967 when the McDonnell Aircraft Co of St. Louis, merged with Douglas Aircraft Co of Long Beach, Calif.
